tracks.title: Earth at night
tracks.subtitle: City lights 2012 to 2023, then what changed
tracks.description: One slow scan across the Earth at night for each year from 2012 to 2023: bright cities ring notes, a deep hum follows all the light. Then NASA's map of what changed, heard as the decade: one note per year, higher as the light grows.
tracks.units: share of the brightest light (years); change in light (the change map)

words.subject: planet
words.missing: not read. The far north and Antarctica are left out, because ice and snow there look like light.

tracks.summary: A slow scan line moves west to east across the Earth at night, once for each year from 2012 to 2023. Then NASA's map of how the lights changed is heard as the decade, one note per year.
tracks.viewsMethod: Region: instead of the whole map, hear one of the four places NASA zooms in on in this video, year by year and then its decade. The scan line then crosses only that region, more slowly, and the notes and the ears stretch to fit it: its north edge plays the highest notes, in your left ear. Zoomed in, dimmer towns ring notes too.

about.what: Earth's city lights, one scan for each year from 2012 to 2023, and then how they changed: lights that grew and lights that dimmed.
about.who: NASA's Black Marble team, with the VIIRS instrument on the Suomi NPP satellite (NASA and NOAA). Kel Elkins made the Earth Information Center version at NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio.
about.where: The whole world, and the four close-ups NASA draws: Western Europe, the Eastern Mediterranean, Ukraine and India.
about.why: To hear where people's light grew or faded over a decade, and by how much.
about.how: A scan line crosses the map from west to east once for each year, and bright cities ring notes. The last map is the decade: one note per year, an octave higher for twice the light, then a rising, falling or single note for what NASA's change map shows.

tracks.title: Air quality
tracks.subtitle: Four pollutants, summer 2024
tracks.description: NASA's model of the air we breathe in July and August 2024, a summer of huge wildfires. One scan for each pollutant: fine particles, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and ozone. Clean air is a calm drone; dirty air rings notes and turns the drone sour.
tracks.units: position on NASA's colour scale for that pollutant

words.subject: planet
words.missing: not read. NASA's model has no reading here.

about.what: Four pollutants in the air over the whole world: fine particles (PM2.5), carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and ozone, in a summer of huge wildfires.
about.who: NASA's Global Modeling and Assimilation Office runs the GEOS-CF system that models them. NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio made the maps.
about.where: The whole world, one map for each pollutant.
about.why: To hear that the air we breathe is shared, and how smoke and pollution spread.
about.how: Clean air is a calm drone. Where a pollutant is thickest, notes ring and the drone turns a little sour.

tracks.title: Ocean currents
tracks.subtitle: Surface currents, 2007 to 2008
tracks.description: Starts with a guided lesson: what a current is, then the Gulf Stream's direction, speed and changes, one idea at a time. Then a scan line crosses NASA's world map of the ocean's surface currents, March 2007 to March 2008: only what is under the line plays.

words.subject: ocean
words.missing: land, or too far north, so there is no current reading here. Try a place at sea.

about.what: NASA's world map of the ocean's surface currents from March 2007 to March 2008, after a guided lesson on the Gulf Stream from NASA's Perpetual Ocean 2 film.
about.who: Greg Shirah, Horace Mitchell and Eric Sokolowsky at NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio, with scientists Hong Zhang (UCLA) and Dimitris Menemenlis (NASA JPL). The currents come from the ECCO2 ocean model.
about.when: The map: March 2007 to March 2008, averaged over the year. The lesson: 17 March to 19 June 2023, from NASA's Perpetual Ocean 2 film.
about.where: The whole world ocean. The lesson follows the Gulf Stream from Miami to the open Atlantic.
about.why: To hear where the strong, fast currents run, like the Gulf Stream and the Kuroshio, which carry warm water around the planet.
about.how: The lesson first explains direction and speed, one sound at a time. Then a scan line crosses the map west to east: a harp rings where it crosses a strong current, and a low hum follows all the moving water under it.

tracks.subtitle: Seven weeks of early 2020
tracks.description: NASA's model of carbon dioxide on a turning globe. A scan line runs pole to pole; the hum is the carbon dioxide on it, and turns tense over dense plumes. A soft heartbeat marks each day.
tracks.units: share of the densest carbon dioxide

about.who: AJ Christensen and the team at NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio, with scientific consulting by Lesley Ott. The data is a global model run in the DYAMOND project.
about.where: The whole globe, seen as it turns.
about.why: To hear how carbon dioxide builds up and travels, and where it is densest.
about.how: A scan line runs pole to pole on the turning globe. The hum is the carbon dioxide on it, and turns tense over dense plumes. A soft heartbeat marks each day.

tracks.title: Lightning
tracks.subtitle: 2017 to 2023, in 14 parts
tracks.description: Lightning seen from the International Space Station, March 2017 to July 2023, in 14 parts, in order. A deep bass swells with all the lightning under the scan line, strings rise as the storms move north, and a harp plucks the strongest storms.

about.who: The Lightning Imaging Sensor on the space station. Michala Garrison made the visualization at NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio.
about.where: Everywhere the sensor can see, about 55 degrees north to 55 degrees south.
about.why: To hear where the storms are, and how the busiest regions swing north and south through the seasons.
about.how: A deep bass swells with how much lightning is under the scan line, strings rise as storms move north, and a harp plucks the strongest storms.

tracks.title: Aerosols
tracks.subtitle: Four winds, 19 August 2025
tracks.description: NASA's model of the aerosols in the air at one moment, scanned once, slowly. Each aerosol is its own wind: rough smoke, sandy dust, low sea salt and thin, high sulfate. Listen to all four, or to one at a time.
tracks.units: share of the thickest places of each aerosol
tracks.viewsMethod: NASA's stories: instead of the whole map, hear the six events NASA describes on this map, one after another. The scan line crosses only a window around each event, more slowly. The wind of the aerosol NASA names for it is brought forward, and the others stay, a little softer. Inside a window, high and low and the two ears stretch to fit it.

about.what: Four kinds of tiny particles in the air at one moment: smoke (black carbon), dust, sea salt and sulfate, and six stories NASA tells about them.
about.who: NASA's Global Modeling and Assimilation Office ran the GEOS model. Joseph V. Ardizzone and Helen-Nicole Kostis made the visualization, with scientist Lesley Ott.
about.when: 19 August 2025, 20:00 UTC: one moment, not an average.
about.where: The whole world. NASA's stories are Hurricane Erin, dust from the Sahara, Kilauea, Etna, smoke over southern Africa and wildfires in Spain.
about.why: To hear that the air is shared: smoke, dust and salt cross oceans and borders.
about.how: Each aerosol is its own wind, louder where there is more of it. In NASA's stories the aerosol NASA names also plays its own instrument.

tracks.title: Warm and cold seas
tracks.subtitle: Sea surface temperature, March 2007 to March 2008
tracks.description: NASA's model of the ocean's surface currents, coloured by temperature, over one year. A level scan line moves down the map from the Arctic to Antarctica, once each season, with west in your left ear and east in your right. Cold sea is a deep base note; the warmer the water, the more and higher chord voices join it.
tracks.units: degrees Celsius, read from NASA's colour key

words.subject: ocean
words.missing: not read: NASA draws no current here, so it is land, sea ice or Antarctica.

tracks.summary: A level scan line moves down NASA's map of the ocean's surface, from the Arctic to Antarctica, once for each quarter of the year from March 2007 to March 2008.

about.what: How warm the ocean's surface is, as NASA's flow lines show it, from the Arctic to Antarctica, in four seasons.
about.who: Greg Shirah and colleagues at NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio, with scientists Hong Zhang and Dimitris Menemenlis. The currents and temperatures come from the ECCO2 ocean model (NASA and JPL).
about.where: The global ocean. Land and sea ice have no flow lines, so no reading.
about.why: To hear the shape of the ocean's warmth: the hot tropics, the cold poles, the Gulf Stream's warm tongue.
about.how: A level scan line moves down the map. Each stretch plays a bell note whose pitch is the water's temperature: warmer sounds higher. Cold sea is a deep base note, and the warmer the water, the more chord voices join it.

tracks.title: El Niño: then and now
tracks.subtitle: Sea temperature, 2025 and 2026
tracks.description: NASA's map of how much warmer or cooler than normal the sea is, one map a month: each month of 2025, then the same month of 2026. A rising pair of notes is sea much warmer than normal; a low falling cello, much cooler. Listen to the middle of the Pacific: in 2026, El Niño warms it.

words.subject: ocean
words.map: map of sea temperature compared with normal
words.missing: land or sea ice, so there is no sea temperature here. Try a place at sea.

about.what: NASA's map of how much warmer or cooler than normal the sea surface is, one map a month: each month of 2025, then the same month of 2026.
about.who: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio, from the MUR sea surface temperature data of NASA JPL's PO.DAAC.
about.when: January to November 2025, each month followed by the same month of 2026.
about.where: The world ocean. El Niño shows in the central and eastern tropical Pacific.
about.why: El Niño warms the tropical Pacific and shifts heat and rain around the world. Hearing a month of 2025 next to the same month of 2026 makes the change stand out.
about.how: A scan line crosses each map west to east. A rising pair of notes rings where the sea is much warmer than normal, a low cello falls where it is much cooler, and a deep hum grows with how far from normal the sea under the line is.
